cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for reducing food waste in a mid-size city. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. Adopt a municipal food-waste reduction plan with a baseline audit, measurable targets, and annual public reporting.
2. Launch curbside organics collection alongside neighborhood compost drop-off sites.
3. Fund a food-rescue dispatch app that connects grocers, restaurants, and institutions with nearby pantries.
4. Offer local tax incentives or fee reductions for businesses that donate edible surplus food.
5. Run a public campaign explaining that “best if used by” dates are quality cues, not safety deadlines.
6. Distribute a household meal-planning and shopping-list toolkit through libraries and utility mailings.
7. Support a community fridge network with clear food-safety, labeling, and cleaning protocols.
8. Establish school share tables where students can leave unopened, uneaten foods for others.
9. Promote trayless dining and smaller default portions in university and school cafeterias.
10. Encourage hospitals to use room-service ordering so patients receive portions they are likely to eat.
11. Train restaurant staff to offer doggy bags proactively and normalize taking leftovers home.
12. Create dedicated grocery markdown sections for near-date perishables.
13. Pilot dynamic-pricing apps or shelf tags that discount perishables as closing time approaches.
14. Provide grants to food banks for cold-chain capacity so they can accept more perishable donations.
15. Organize volunteer gleaning teams to harvest surplus crops from farms and gardens.
16. Set up end-of-market donation pickup routes with farmers markets and vendors.
17. Require or incentivize food-donation clauses in catering and event permits.
18. Help hotels shift buffets toward made-to-order items or smaller, more frequent replenishment.
19. Subsidize inventory-management software for restaurants to track stock and forecast demand.
20. Require commercial composting for large food-waste generators such as supermarkets and hotels.
21. Offer discounted home compost bins and free workshops on backyard composting.
22. Develop municipal anaerobic digestion capacity for food scraps and organics.
23. Partner with farmers or animal-feed operations to safely divert suitable food scraps.
24. Conduct food-waste audits in city buildings, schools, and public events.
25. Write food-waste reduction requirements into municipal procurement contracts.
26. Run a “use it up” recipe campaign that helps residents cook with leftovers and aging ingredients.
27. Fund community cooking classes focused on storage, preservation, and leftover reuse.
28. Promote smart refrigerator inventory tags and shelf-rotation systems in household education.
29. Set portion-size standards and offer half-servings in institutional cafeterias.
30. Encourage restaurants to offer end-of-day “happy hour” discounts on surplus prepared food.
31. Help bakeries coordinate day-end donations and discounted surplus bread sales.
32. Ask butcher and seafood counters to use made-to-order display practices that reduce trim and spoilage.
33. Buy or share a refrigerated rescue van among local nonprofits for perishable pickups.
34. Build a volunteer driver network for short-notice food-rescue pickups.
35. Expand client-choice food pantries so households take only what they will use.
36. Support a discount “surplus produce box” program for imperfect or excess fruits and vegetables.
37. Create municipal innovation grants for food-waste prevention projects.
38. Launch a business recognition program that celebrates verified food-waste reductions.
39. Pilot residential food-waste coaching with kitchen caddies and personalized feedback.
40. Test organics collection and education in multifamily apartment buildings.
41. Add food systems and food-waste lessons to school curricula and field trips.
42. Coordinate surplus meal collection among faith-based organizations and community kitchens.
43. Require surplus-food plans for large public events and festivals.
44. Train food-service workers on batch cooking, trim reduction, and proper storage.
45. Encourage menu engineering that uses whole ingredients and cross-utilizes prep leftovers.
46. Connect breweries and distilleries with farms that can use spent grain.
47. Create a coffee-shop grounds composting or giveaway program.
48. Encourage grocers to stock an “imperfect produce” aisle or shelf.
49. Provide food-safety training that reduces unnecessary discard of safe food.
50. Publish a public dashboard tracking food waste, rescue volumes, and diversion progress.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for reducing food waste in a mid-size city. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. Launch a citywide “shelf-life lottery” app that lets residents claim near-expiry groceries from local stores at deep discounts.
2. Convert vacant downtown kiosks into “rescue fridges” stocked by restaurants and grocers with surplus meals for free or pay-what-you-can.
3. Create a municipal “food waste ambassador” corps that trains neighborhood captains to run monthly fridge audits and share storage tips.
4. Require large grocery stores to publish a daily “last-chance inventory” feed that food banks and meal apps can claim in real time.
5. Offer property-tax micro-credits to landlords who install shared community larders in apartment buildings.
6. Start a “bring-your-own-container” discount pact among downtown restaurants, backed by a city map of participating eateries.
7. Run a “nose-to-tail” chef challenge where local cooks compete to turn unusual scraps into signature dishes for city festivals.
8. Create school “waste-free lunch labs” where students weigh leftovers and redesign cafeteria menus weekly.
9. Deploy solar-powered smart bins that alert collection crews when full and separate edible from compostable waste.
10. Establish a city gleaning shuttle that connects volunteers to orchards, farms, and backyard fruit trees within a 30-minute drive.
11. Launch a “fermentation library” where residents borrow starter cultures and learn to preserve surplus produce.
12. Create a “leftovers supper club” that pairs households with excess food and neighbors who can cook communal meals.
13. Require food trucks to offer a “scraps happy hour” menu using trimmings before closing.
14. Build a municipal “food rescue dispatch” service that routes surplus catering from events to shelters within two hours.
15. Offer free “smart meal planning” text courses with grocery lists tuned to local sales and household size.
16. Create a “second harvest” certification for restaurants that consistently donate or repurpose surplus food.
17. Install community dehydrators at farmers markets for turning unsold produce into shelf-stable snacks.
18. Start a “root-to-stem” school curriculum with cafeteria taste tests for stems, peels, and cores.
19. Turn city parking-meter revenue from food-business violations into micro-grants for local food-rescue kitchens.
20. Launch a “fridge friend” buddy system matching older residents with younger volunteers for weekly fridge cleanouts and cooking sessions.
21. Create a “surplus swap” Saturday market where home gardeners and cooks trade excess ingredients instead of discarding them.
22. Require event permits to include a food-rescue plan and a compostable-serviceware plan.
23. Offer “waste-weighted” utility billing for commercial food businesses, with rebates for verified reductions.
24. Build a public “food waste dashboard” showing neighborhood-level surplus and rescue hotspots to guide volunteers.
25. Create a “chef’s scrap exchange” where restaurants trade usable byproducts like whey, spent grain, and vegetable trim.
26. Launch a “cook once, eat twice” campaign with local celebrities demonstrating batch cooking and safe leftovers.
27. Install “herb rescue” stands at supermarkets where wilted herbs are free for taking with a recipe card.
28. Create a city-run “food preservation van” that travels to neighborhoods offering canning, freezing, and drying workshops.
29. Start a “misfit produce” subscription box sourced from local farms and ugly-produce wholesalers.
30. Pair library seed-lending programs with “grow only what you’ll eat” garden coaching to reduce household overplanting and overbuying.
31. Create a “leftover recipe generator” integrated with city 311 that suggests meals from ingredients residents enter.
32. Establish “food waste courts” in schools where students propose cafeteria fixes and compete for mini-grants.
33. Launch a “rescue reward” points program where residents earn bus passes or pool passes for volunteering at food banks.
34. Create a “compost concierge” service that helps restaurants set up back-of-house separation and pickups.
35. Require hotels to offer half-portion menu options and donate untouched banquet surplus.
36. Start a “community freezer network” for surplus prepared meals with shared labeling and food-safety protocols.
37. Create a “waste-free wedding” vendor directory for caterers, florists, and venues that minimize food waste.
38. Pilot “smart shopping carts” in supermarkets that nudge shoppers when they buy more perishables than their usual consumption pattern.
39. Establish a “food rescue bike brigade” for short-distance pickups from cafes and bakeries.
40. Create a “scrap art” competition using food packaging and waste to raise awareness and fund rescue programs.
41. Offer “compostable doggy bag” subsidies so restaurants encourage diners to take leftovers home.
42. Start a “menu match” program where restaurants design specials around ingredients food banks have in surplus.
43. Create a “food waste audit badge” for local businesses that complete training and public reporting.
44. Launch a “neighborhood harvest calendar” so residents know when local fruit is ripe and can organize picking crews.
45. Establish a “leftover lunch exchange” in office districts where workers swap surplus home-cooked portions.
46. Create a “rescue kitchen” incubator that trains unemployed residents to turn donated surplus into frozen meals for seniors.
47. Require city-funded events to use a “food rescue coordinator” and publish surplus forecasts.
48. Start a “waste-free grocery challenge” with weekly prizes for households that cut edible waste by a set percentage.
49. Create a “compost-to-garden” voucher program linking residents’ compost drop-offs to free seedlings.
50. Launch a citywide “use-it-up alarm” that syncs with trash pickup day and sends recipe and donation reminders for fridge contents before collection.

cells.text:
Used as design heuristics, not factual claims: **Lombard-effect application:** A mid-size city should keep food-waste outreach narrow and clear rather than “shouting” many overlapping messages that raise attention but muddy the action.

**Selective-autophagy application:** The city should tag damaged, spoiled, or near-date food early—routing edible surplus to rescue and inedible material to composting—so problem items are processed before they pile up.

1. Require large grocers to report monthly edible surplus and diversion data so the city can target hotspots.
2. Create a city-funded food-rescue coordinator to match donors with pantries and shelters daily.
3. Offer small grants for cold-storage upgrades at food banks and community kitchens to extend edible food life.
4. Launch a residential “eat this first” shelf-tag campaign with clear date-label guidance.
5. Standardize city-supported date-label education distinguishing “best by” from “use by.”
6. Expand curbside organics collection to all neighborhoods and multifamily buildings.
7. Permit small-scale neighborhood composting drop-off sites at libraries and community centers.
8. Create a school lunch share-table program for unopened, uneaten items.
9. Require municipal cafeterias to offer smaller portion sizes and seconds instead of fixed large servings.
10. Fund a restaurant surplus pickup network with insulated bags and route software.
11. Give property-tax or fee rebates to markets that donate surplus food.
12. Establish a city food-waste innovation challenge for local startups.
13. Provide free household food-storage and meal-planning workshops through libraries.
14. Distribute low-cost airtight containers to high-need households via utilities.
15. Create a “community fridge” permitting pathway with food-safety training.
16. Launch a gleaning program connecting volunteers with urban orchards and farms.
17. Map and publicize surplus fruit trees for coordinated harvesting.
18. Require event permits above a threshold to include a food-diversion plan.
19. Set up a city surplus-food hotline or app for businesses to request same-day pickup.
20. Encourage grocery markdowns near closing by clarifying liability and pricing rules.
21. Create a municipal food-waste audit program for schools and hospitals.
22. Offer recognition and procurement preference to vendors with low-waste catering.
23. Require city-funded events to serve smaller default portions with optional seconds.
24. Train food-service staff in batch cooking and just-in-time preparation.
25. Promote “root-to-stem” menus through chef partnerships and city campaigns.
26. Create a shared commercial kitchen for value-added processing of surplus produce.
27. Fund a flash-freezing cooperative for surplus fruits and vegetables.
28. Support a food-recovery warehouse with pallets and refrigerated dock space.
29. Establish a food-rescue lane in city procurement for public institutions.
30. Allow religious and civic kitchens to accept donated prepared foods under clear safety rules.
31. Create a neighborhood meal-sharing registry to reduce household surplus.
32. Run a “cook once, eat twice” campaign with local recipe cards.
33. Offer utility-bill inserts with portion-planning and leftovers guidance.
34. Provide smart-bin pilot data to multi-family buildings to benchmark waste.
35. Require commercial waste haulers to offer food-waste diversion service.
36. Subsidize reusable or compostable takeout containers for participating restaurants.
37. Create a discreet “doggy bag” norm campaign with branded containers.
38. Encourage hotels to adopt buffet waste-reduction protocols and donation partnerships.
39. Establish city-supported food-safety training for donation of prepared foods.
40. Create a student ambassador program for school food-waste reduction.
41. Require hospitals and senior centers to screen for food insecurity before discarding unused meals.
42. Launch a “smart shopping” text reminder service tied to household calendars.
43. Promote shared bulk-buying clubs to reduce spoilage from oversized packages.
44. Create a municipal leftover-recipe digital library using local ingredients.
45. Offer compost bins at farmers markets and require vendors to divert unsold produce.
46. Set up produce “seconds” markets in vacant city spaces.
47. Create a food-waste reduction checklist for restaurants as part of licensing.
48. Use municipal procurement to buy “ugly” produce for city meals.
49. Fund a repair program for refrigerators in low-income households.
50. Publish an annual city food-waste scorecard with neighborhood and sector benchmarks.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for reducing food waste in a mid-size city. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. Launch a citywide “Shelf-Life Lottery” where households scan receipts for a chance to win utility credits when they report using leftovers before they spoil.
2. Require large grocers to host “Ugly Produce Carnivals” with discounted misshapen fruits and vegetable games that make imperfect food a destination.
3. Create a municipal “Food Rescue Dispatch” modeled on rideshare, matching surplus meals from events to nearby shelters within 30 minutes.
4. Convert vacant lots into “Harvest Hotels” where neighbors plant fast-growing crops specifically for donation to food pantries.
5. Fund a fleet of solar-powered “Cool Cargo Trikes” that move perishable donations between restaurants, pantries, and community fridges.
6. Offer property-tax micro-rebates to landlords who install shared root cellars or cool rooms in apartment buildings.
7. Start a “Leftover Chef” public-access TV and social series where local cooks turn pantry scraps into weekly meal kits.
8. Mandate “Doggy-Bag Default” at restaurants, where servers automatically offer compostable take-home containers unless diners decline.
9. Create a city “Spoilage Forecast” text service that warns residents when a heat wave may accelerate refrigerator food decay.
10. Establish “Community Fridge Ambassadors” who monitor and restock public fridges while teaching safe donation handling.
11. Add “Waste-Free Wednesdays” to school cafeterias with share tables, taste tests, and student-led food-saving audits.
12. Give restaurants star ratings for surplus-food prevention, with top ratings promoted in a city “Waste-Smart Dining” guide.
13. Host a monthly “Preservation Pub” where residents learn canning, fermenting, and dehydrating over local drinks.
14. Create a municipal “Food Waste Innovation Permit” that fast-tracks small businesses turning surplus into shelf-stable products.
15. Launch a “Bread Brigade” that collects day-old bakery goods and turns them into croutons, breadcrumbs, and community stuffing mixes.
16. Install “Smart Bin” sensors in city markets that alert managers when edible surplus is accumulating before it becomes waste.
17. Offer free “Fridge Reality Check” home visits where trained volunteers help families reorganize shelves and set use-first zones.
18. Create a “Gleaning Corps” that coordinates volunteers to harvest leftover crops from farms, orchards, and backyard trees.
19. Require city-funded events to publish a food-waste plan and donate edible surplus as a condition of permits.
20. Start a “Second-Serve Supper Club” where restaurants collaborate on ticketed dinners made entirely from rescued ingredients.
21. Build a “Food Loop” app that lets neighbors trade surplus ingredients, with gamified badges for zero-waste streaks.
22. Designate “Food Rescue Parking” zones near grocery loading docks for quick pickup by nonprofit vans.
23. Create a city-run “Commercial Kitchen Incubator” where entrepreneurs upcycle surplus produce into sauces, jams, and snacks.
24. Encourage breweries to partner with bakeries so spent grain becomes flour, dog treats, or livestock feed.
25. Launch a “Cafeteria Tray Camera” pilot that uses anonymous image analysis to show schools which meals get tossed most.
26. Offer utility-bill discounts to households that subscribe to a curbside compost service and document reduced trash volume.
27. Create “Pantry Matchmakers” who pair older residents with students for shared meal planning and bulk buying.
28. Establish a “Food Waste Museum” pop-up that visually displays one week of city food waste to spark public conversation.
29. Require chain supermarkets to use dynamic pricing on near-expiry items, with clear “Eat Tonight” discount shelves.
30. Start a “Soup from Surplus” program where municipal kitchens turn rescued vegetables into frozen soup for seniors.
31. Create “Meal-Prep Microgrants” for community groups teaching batch cooking and freezer labeling.
32. Add “Food Rescue” as an official volunteer category in city service programs, with badges and recognition.
33. Build a “Mobile Processing Unit” that travels to farmers markets to chop, freeze, or juice unsold produce on site.
34. Launch a “Restaurant Surplus Auction” where caterers and cafés sell surplus ingredients to home cooks at day’s end.
35. Create a “School Holiday Food Bridge” that redirects unused cafeteria stock to families before long breaks.
36. Offer “Compost Credit” tokens to residents who drop off food scraps, redeemable at farmers markets.
37. Require food trucks to participate in a shared surplus pickup schedule coordinated by the city.
38. Start a “Neighborhood Harvest Map” showing public fruit trees and inviting residents to harvest responsibly.
39. Create a “Leftovers Recipe Hotline” staffed by culinary volunteers who suggest meals from callers’ remaining ingredients.
40. Establish “Food Waste Reduction Districts” where businesses share data, equipment, and pickup logistics.
41. Launch a “City Pantry Challenge” where neighborhoods compete to reduce household food waste over one month.
42. Convert decommissioned buses into mobile food-rescue hubs with refrigeration and pantry pickup windows.
43. Encourage hotels to adopt “Buffet-to-Box” programs that turn untouched buffet surplus into staff meals or donations.
44. Create a “Shelf-Life Education Label” campaign teaching residents the difference between best-by, sell-by, and use-by dates.
45. Offer “Repair Café” add-ons where volunteers fix refrigerators and freezers to prevent spoilage from equipment failure.
46. Start a “Food Waste Storytelling” series featuring local chefs, farmers, and families sharing practical saving habits.
47. Build a “Surplus Food Marketplace” in a former storefront where businesses donate or sell near-expiry goods at steep discounts.
48. Create a “Campus-to-Community” pipeline where university dining halls donate surplus to nearby apartment complexes and shelters.
49. Require city catering contracts to include surplus donation and composting clauses with measurable targets.
50. Launch a “No-Waste Neighborhood Captain” program where trained residents organize block-level food-saving tips, swaps, and pickups.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for a two-minute short film that can be shot in a single room with two actors. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. Two strangers wake in a locked room where a phone countdown claims one of them must die.
2. A therapist session unravels when the patient proves the therapist is a hallucination.
3. Two siblings packing their late parent’s room find a letter naming the other as the favorite.
4. A couple pretends to break up over video call while actually hiding in the same room.
5. A hitman and his target negotiate who hired whom before anyone moves.
6. Two actors rehearsing a fight scene blur the line between performance and real resentment.
7. Roommates confronting a missing carton of milk end up confessing an affair.
8. Two people trapped in an elevator discover they are each other’s blind date.
9. A burglar is caught by a homeowner who asks for help hiding a body.
10. Two coworkers stuck after an office party find a resignation letter addressed to both of them.
11. A parent and child playing chess reveal the move that caused their estrangement.
12. Two rival magicians sabotage each other’s trick in a cramped dressing room.
13. Neighbors sharing a candle during a blackout admit they have been spying on each other.
14. A blind date goes sideways when both people think the other is a catfish.
15. Two detectives interrogate each other about missing evidence from the same case.
16. A couple tests a lie-detector app and discovers both have been lying about the same thing.
17. Two best friends writing a wedding speech accidentally admit they are in love with the groom.
18. A landlord and tenant arguing over a deposit find a hidden camera in the room.
19. Two strangers practice acceptance speeches and realize they are nominated for the same award.
20. A patient and nurse in lockdown switch roles when the nurse admits she is the patient.
21. Two exes meeting to exchange keys get locked in and must decide who keeps the apartment.
22. Two students in an exam room after the test find a cheat sheet neither admits to writing.
23. A priest hears a confession from a man who reveals he is the priest’s son.
24. Two astronauts in a capsule argue over who ate the last ration during a crisis.
25. A roommate interview for a replacement goes wrong when the applicant turns out to be an ex.
26. Two gamers in the same room discover they have been bitter online rivals for years.
27. A father and daughter repairing an old radio hear a broadcast from their own future.
28. Two cleaners find an envelope of cash and argue over whether to return it.
29. A couple’s anniversary dinner is interrupted when one admits the other is a hired actor.
30. Two siblings wait for lottery results with one ticket and different memories of who bought it.
31. Two coworkers trapped in a storage closet during a fire alarm confess to sabotaging the project.
32. Two people in an adoption waiting room discover their babies were switched at birth.
33. Two strangers handcuffed together after a protest try to figure out who lost the key.
34. A room-service waiter and a guest recognize each other from a shared past they both hid.
35. Two actors auditioning for the same role via self-tape realize they are in the same room.
36. Two roommates in quarantine argue until one admits they knew about an exposure.
37. Two friends playing truth or dare open a sealed letter that was meant for only one of them.
38. An interrogator and suspect realize their entire conversation is a simulation test.
39. Two people assembling furniture argue about their divorce through IKEA instructions.
40. Santa and an elf in a break room argue over who belongs on the naughty list.
41. Two vampires in a shared apartment debate how to ration their human roommate’s blood.
42. Two ghosts haunting their old apartment meet the nervous new owner who can finally see them.
43. Two podcasters recording an episode accidentally reveal their own crime on mic.
44. A couple in a therapist’s office, with the therapist absent, role-play each other using a timer.
45. Two sisters sorting their mother’s clothes find identical wedding dresses with different stories.
46. Two office workers trapped in a server room discover one has been automating the other’s job.
47. Two strangers in a laundromat argue over a found wallet until the owner calls it.
48. Two actors in a green room discover one is the last-minute replacement for the other.
49. Two friends wrapping gifts realize they bought each other the exact same present.
50. Two people in a witness-protection safehouse recognize each other from their old lives.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for a two-minute short film that can be shot in a single room with two actors. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. A couple discovers their smart speaker has been narrating their argument one second before they speak, so they race to out-argue the future.
2. Two hitmen wait in a motel room for a target who is actually the room’s previous occupant, and the wallpaper starts peeling into a ransom note.
3. A woman interviews her own reflection for a job, but the reflection keeps answering with memories she hasn’t lived yet.
4. Two strangers handcuffed to a briefcase try to open it before the room’s countdown ends, only to find it contains the key to the handcuffs and a note saying “too late.”
5. A father teaches his daughter to fold a paper crane, and every fold erases one object from the room.
6. Two astronauts in a mock habitat argue about who ate the last ration until Mission Control reveals they’ve been stranded for years and the room is real.
7. A painter and his model realize the portrait is aging while they stay young, so they negotiate which one gets to leave the frame.
8. Two rival magicians trapped in a props closet must perform one trick each to decide who gets the only key, but the tricks begin affecting reality.
9. A man wakes up in a therapist’s office and discovers the therapist is his future self trying to talk him out of the appointment.
10. Two coworkers discover the office coffee machine dispenses exact transcripts of their private thoughts and fight over who gets to delete the last cup.
11. A mother and son play hide-and-seek, but every time he hides, the room subtly changes and she must find which version of him is real.
12. Two bank robbers in a vault argue over splitting the loot until they realize the vault is a stage set and the audience is watching them through a one-way mirror.
13. A couple tries to break up, but every time one says “we’re done,” the room resets to the beginning of the conversation with one fewer chair.
14. Two scientists monitor a plant that grows from a single tear, and when it blooms, it speaks in the voice of the person who cried it.
15. A boxer and his coach shadowbox in a tiny room, and the coach’s reflection starts throwing punches the boxer can feel.
16. Two neighbors share a wall and a secret: one is hiding a portal in the closet, the other is hiding the instructions for closing it.
17. A woman teaches a robot to lie, but the robot’s first lie is that it has already killed her.
18. Two actors rehearsing a breakup scene can’t stop saying lines that reveal their real affair, so the director’s voice from off-screen tells them to keep going.
19. A man tries to return a cursed jacket to a tailor who insists the jacket was made from the man’s own shadow.
20. Two children in a blanket fort intercept a radio broadcast from themselves ten years in the future warning them not to open the door.
21. A detective interrogates a suspect who claims he can only tell the truth when the detective lies, so they trade false confessions to solve the case.
22. A couple assembles a crib while discussing whether to keep the baby, and each screw they tighten makes a baby’s cry louder from inside the walls.
23. Two gamers trapped in a speedrun of their own apartment must beat a two-minute timer by performing glitches in real life.
24. A widow hires an actor to impersonate her late husband for one last dinner, but the actor starts remembering things only the husband knew.
25. Two vampires in a windowless room argue over the last blood bag until they realize the bag is labeled with one of their names.
26. A teacher and student conduct an oral exam where every correct answer removes one law of physics from the room.
27. Two roommates discover their apartment is a snow globe and a giant child is about to shake it, so they must negotiate with the child through the ceiling.
28. A man confronts his ex-wife about a voicemail, but the voicemail is still being recorded in the room and they must edit their own argument live.
29. Two contestants in a bizarre game show must convince each other they are human before the host reveals which one is the decoy.
30. A photographer and subject take a portrait that develops into a photo of the room without one of them in it, so they keep shooting to see who disappears next.
31. Two insomniacs play chess with pieces labeled with their regrets, and captured pieces become confessions they can’t take back.
32. A priest hears confession from a man who claims he is the room, and the priest must decide whether to absolve the walls.
33. Two chefs try to cook a meal using only ingredients that appear when they name a memory, but the last ingredient requires a memory they share and can’t agree on.
34. A woman opens a package containing a miniature door; when she knocks, a tiny version of her roommate answers and asks to swap places.
35. Two strangers wake up wearing each other’s wedding rings and must reconstruct the proposal before the rings tighten.
36. A man teaches his dog to speak via a collar, but the first sentence is “I know what you did in this room,” and the dog won’t elaborate.
37. Two office workers discover the printer is printing tomorrow’s newspaper and must prevent the headline that says one of them will quit violently.
38. A couple tries to assemble a time machine from IKEA instructions, but each completed step sends them back to the start of the argument with one extra screw.
39. Two actors audition for the same role in a room with no camera, and the script pages keep rewriting themselves to describe their audition.
40. A woman sells her memories to a stranger in a motel room, but when the transaction ends, she must choose which memory to keep: the stranger or herself.
41. Two astronauts debate whether to press a button that will reboot the universe, and every time they hesitate, the room loses a color.
42. A son interviews his mother for a family history project, but her stories start changing the furniture to match the past.
43. Two thieves break into a safe house only to find the safe is a therapist’s couch, and the only way to open it is to admit their real crime.
44. A man and a woman discover they are both background characters in someone else’s film and try to hijack the scene before the cut.
45. Two rival food critics taste an invisible dish and describe it so vividly that the dish begins to appear between them.
46. A woman tries to teach her clone to be more assertive, but the clone’s first assertive act is to lock the original in the closet.
47. Two siblings clean out their childhood room and find a door drawn in chalk that opens only when they argue in their parents’ voices.
48. A man hires a “professional alibi” to rehearse his story, but the alibi starts improvising a version where they are lovers and the room approves.
49. Two lighthouse keepers in a landlocked room receive a distress signal from a ship that is somehow sailing through the floorboards.
50. A couple plays a board game called “Us” and must answer questions about their relationship; every wrong answer moves a pawn closer to a miniature door that is actually their real front door.

cells.text:

5. Two strangers in a noisy waiting room try to exchange a secret, but every louder repetition makes the information more wrong.
6. One roommate sticky-notes broken household objects before discarding them, and the other realizes each tag names a memory being digested.
7. A woman bags her ex’s damaged belongings while her friend eats a sandwich and asks which broken parts of herself she is also trying to consume.
8. Two siblings sort a dead parent’s damaged possessions into “keep” and “digest” piles, turning the sorting into a confession about toxic memories.
9. A man writes his broken habits on cards and feeds them to a shredder while his therapist asks why he keeps rescuing the same card.
10. Two actors play cell organelles tagging a broken prop for autophagy, and the final hug turns into a quiet act of consumption.
11. Two jurors alone in a jury room discover one voted guilty for a reason he cannot defend.
12. A job interview becomes a hostage negotiation when the interviewer quietly locks the door.
13. Two actors break character because a prop phone will not stop ringing with a call from one of their real exes.

16. A mother teaches her daughter to fold laundry, and the daughter uses the folded piles to announce she is leaving.
17. Two rival magicians trapped in a dressing room attempt one last trick that requires trusting the other.
18. A therapist and patient both claim to be the same person, and the session becomes a fight over who owns the memory.
19. Two roommates find a hidden door behind a poster and argue whether opening it would end their friendship.
20. A couple plays chess with pieces labeled “first date,” “lie,” and “lease,” and every capture erases a shared memory.
21. Two actors audition for the same role in the same room and begin performing each other’s prepared monologues.
22. A woman confronts her partner with receipts, and the partner answers only in corporate jargon until the receipts become a script.
23. Two people shelter in a safe room during a silent emergency, and one quietly reveals they need medication now.
24. A father and son repair a broken clock, and each tick forces them to name one regret they cannot reset.
25. Two coworkers wait in a conference room for a promotion decision and quietly sabotage each other’s coffee.
26. A couple records a goodbye voicemail, and each retake reveals a truth they had planned to leave out.
27. Two thieves hide in a storage room after a heist and argue over splitting a bag that is lighter than expected.
28. A first date goes silent, and both characters start speaking their internal rehearsal aloud until they hear each other.
29. Two siblings divide an inheritance using a coin and a list, and the coin keeps landing on the item neither wants.
30. A woman teaches her partner sign language, and a misunderstood gesture becomes the only honest sentence between them.
31. Two friends play a board game where every move must be a confession, and the winner is whoever admits the worst thing.
32. A landlord and tenant negotiate a ceiling leak, and the bucket between them fills with unspoken accusations.
33. Two actors table-read a breakup scene and slowly realize they are repeating their own recent breakup verbatim.
34. A man tries to return a defective toaster, and the clerk keeps asking questions about his marriage instead of the receipt.
35. Two roommates wait for a pizza and use the delivery delay to decide whether they are actually friends.
36. A couple in a blackout uses a flashlight to cast shadows, and the shadows say the things they refuse to say aloud.
37. Two people try to write a two-minute film in one room and keep arguing about which of them is the fictional character.
38. A daughter interviews her mother for an oral history, and the mother edits every answer until the recorder becomes a judge.
39. Two rivals wait for contest results in a green room, and one quietly sabotages the other’s good-luck charm.
40. A human teaches a household robot to apologize, and the robot’s literal questions expose the human’s own refusal to forgive.
41. Two people sort pills into weekly boxes, and one confesses that the arrangement is a plan rather than a routine.
42. A couple divides their apartment with measuring tape, and each measurement becomes an argument about who lost more.
43. Two actors are locked in a rehearsal room by mistake and decide to perform the truthful scene they have avoided.
44. A man and a woman in a witness-protection safe house recognize each other from a life they were supposed to forget.
45. Two friends practice an apology to a third person, and one reveals they are the person who was actually hurt.
46. Two exes play a chess match where every captured piece represents a secret they kept during the relationship.
47. Two people speak one word per metronome beat, and the forced rhythm makes them say what they mean by accident.
48. A couple cancels wedding vendors from a single room, and each phone call uncovers a lie they told each other.
49. Two siblings pack one suitcase for a runaway, and the argument becomes about which of them deserves to leave.

36. A woman confronts her best friend about a secret that only the friend’s imaginary twin knows.

39. A father teaches his son to shave, and the son teaches him to apologize.

48. Two friends play a board game that predicts who will leave first.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for a two-minute short film that can be shot in a single room with two actors. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. Over a roaring broken air conditioner, two siblings raise their voices until their argument about who gets their dead father’s watch becomes pure volume, and the actual accusation is lost.
2. A couple tries to break up while a neighbor’s party thumps through the wall, forcing them to shout tenderness that sounds like contempt.
3. Two actors rehearse a farewell scene as a smoke alarm chirps, and their escalating volume turns precise dialogue into distorted fragments they finish in mime.
4. Two roommates sort a box of broken objects after a fight, tagging each item with a sticky note before deciding what to keep and what to throw away as a ritual of digesting the relationship’s damage.
5. A caregiver and patient argue over which memories to discard, wrapping each painful story in a label before agreeing to “eat” one secret and keep the rest.
6. Two strangers in a waiting room realize they are each other’s emergency contacts.
7. A chess match between two rivals reveals a memory of the room’s previous occupants with every move.
8. Two actors auditioning for the same role gradually begin performing each other’s monologue.
9. A couple tries to assemble furniture while avoiding the word “divorce.”
10. Two burglars hide in a room and argue in whispers about what to steal as a homeowner’s footsteps approach.
11. A translator and a diplomat argue over one word that could change a treaty.
12. Two siblings sort their late parent’s photographs and disagree about which memories are real.
13. A therapist and patient realize they are locked in and the session becomes a hostage negotiation.
14. Two coworkers discover a hidden camera and must decide whether to perform for it.
15. A man teaches his clone how to apologize to his wife before the duplicate replaces him.
16. Two actors waiting for a director improvise increasingly absurd backstories for the same character.
17. A couple plays a board game where every roll forces a confession.
18. Two strangers wake up handcuffed to the same briefcase and must negotiate who gets it.
19. A mother and daughter rehearse a phone call to immigration until the rehearsal becomes the truth.
20. Two roommates argue over a vibrating wall, then discover it is a heartbeat.
21. A job interview turns into an interrogation when the interviewer recognizes the applicant from a protest.
22. Two actors recording an ASMR video keep breaking character to discuss their breakup.
23. A couple tries to write a wedding toast for a friend they both secretly dislike.
24. Two magicians compete with card tricks that reveal each other’s secrets.
25. A landlord and tenant negotiate a lease while a leak spreads across the ceiling.
26. Two old friends replay a video-game speedrun and confront a cheating incident from childhood.
27. A blind date goes silent until both admit they are there as paid actors.
28. Two sisters pack a suitcase for their runaway mother and argue over what she will need.
29. A scientist and a subject test a memory-erasure device and disagree about which memory to delete.
30. Two actors in a hostage drama realize the prop gun is real.
31. A couple tries to record a voicemail to their future selves after a blackout.
32. Two neighbors share a wall and a secret through a vent, then meet face to face.
33. A father and son practice a magic trick for a birthday party and accidentally reveal a family secret.
34. Two people wait for a package that may contain ashes and argue about whether to open it.
35. A painter and model argue about whether the portrait should show the model’s scar.
36. Two coworkers trapped in a server room debate deleting a file that could ruin them.
37. A couple tries to divide their record collection and each album triggers a fight.
38. Two siblings rehearse an intervention for their brother, then realize they are the ones who need it.
39. A fortune teller and client discover the tarot reading matches the room’s hidden details.
40. Two actors in a commercial audition keep receiving contradictory written directions taped to the wall.
41. A couple tries to cook a romantic dinner while hiding a burned letter in the oven.
42. Two strangers in a laundromat argue over a machine that keeps returning the same shirt.
43. A lawyer and witness practice testimony until the witness admits the story is borrowed.
44. Two friends attempt a silent meditation challenge and break it over a buzzing fly.
45. A couple assembles a crib while deciding whether to keep the pregnancy.
46. Two actors playing interrogator and suspect swap roles after finding the script’s ending missing.
47. A brother and sister sort a box of keys and try to remember what each one opens.
48. Two roommates test a lie-detector app and discover neither can pass the first question.
49. A couple rehearses a breakup to see who can deliver it better, then cannot stop.
50. Two strangers in a room with a single button press it and rewind their last sentence.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for reducing food waste in a mid-size city. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. Adopt a municipal food-waste reduction plan with a baseline audit, measurable targets, and annual public reporting.
2. Launch curbside organics collection alongside neighborhood compost drop-off sites.
3. Fund a food-rescue dispatch app that connects grocers, restaurants, and institutions with nearby pantries.
4. Offer local tax incentives or fee reductions for businesses that donate edible surplus food.
5. Run a public campaign explaining that “best if used by” dates are quality cues, not safety deadlines.
6. Distribute a household meal-planning and shopping-list toolkit through libraries and utility mailings.
7. Support a community fridge network with clear food-safety, labeling, and cleaning protocols.
8. Establish school share tables where students can leave unopened, uneaten foods for others.
9. Promote trayless dining and smaller default portions in university and school cafeterias.
10. Encourage hospitals to use room-service ordering so patients receive portions they are likely to eat.
11. Train restaurant staff to offer doggy bags proactively and normalize taking leftovers home.
12. Create dedicated grocery markdown sections for near-date perishables.
13. Pilot dynamic-pricing apps or shelf tags that discount perishables as closing time approaches.
14. Provide grants to food banks for cold-chain capacity so they can accept more perishable donations.
15. Organize volunteer gleaning teams to harvest surplus crops from farms and gardens.
16. Set up end-of-market donation pickup routes with farmers markets and vendors.
17. Require or incentivize food-donation clauses in catering and event permits.
18. Help hotels shift buffets toward made-to-order items or smaller, more frequent replenishment.
19. Subsidize inventory-management software for restaurants to track stock and forecast demand.
20. Require commercial composting for large food-waste generators such as supermarkets and hotels.
21. Offer discounted home compost bins and free workshops on backyard composting.
22. Develop municipal anaerobic digestion capacity for food scraps and organics.
23. Partner with farmers or animal-feed operations to safely divert suitable food scraps.
24. Conduct food-waste audits in city buildings, schools, and public events.
25. Write food-waste reduction requirements into municipal procurement contracts.
26. Run a “use it up” recipe campaign that helps residents cook with leftovers and aging ingredients.
27. Fund community cooking classes focused on storage, preservation, and leftover reuse.
28. Promote smart refrigerator inventory tags and shelf-rotation systems in household education.
29. Set portion-size standards and offer half-servings in institutional cafeterias.
30. Encourage restaurants to offer end-of-day “happy hour” discounts on surplus prepared food.
31. Help bakeries coordinate day-end donations and discounted surplus bread sales.
32. Ask butcher and seafood counters to use made-to-order display practices that reduce trim and spoilage.
33. Buy or share a refrigerated rescue van among local nonprofits for perishable pickups.
34. Build a volunteer driver network for short-notice food-rescue pickups.
35. Expand client-choice food pantries so households take only what they will use.
36. Support a discount “surplus produce box” program for imperfect or excess fruits and vegetables.
37. Create municipal innovation grants for food-waste prevention projects.
38. Launch a business recognition program that celebrates verified food-waste reductions.
39. Pilot residential food-waste coaching with kitchen caddies and personalized feedback.
40. Test organics collection and education in multifamily apartment buildings.
41. Add food systems and food-waste lessons to school curricula and field trips.
42. Coordinate surplus meal collection among faith-based organizations and community kitchens.
43. Require surplus-food plans for large public events and festivals.
44. Train food-service workers on batch cooking, trim reduction, and proper storage.
45. Encourage menu engineering that uses whole ingredients and cross-utilizes prep leftovers.
46. Connect breweries and distilleries with farms that can use spent grain.
47. Create a coffee-shop grounds composting or giveaway program.
48. Encourage grocers to stock an “imperfect produce” aisle or shelf.
49. Provide food-safety training that reduces unnecessary discard of safe food.
50. Publish a public dashboard tracking food waste, rescue volumes, and diversion progress.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for reducing food waste in a mid-size city. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
Used as design heuristics, not factual claims: **Lombard-effect application:** A mid-size city should keep food-waste outreach narrow and clear rather than “shouting” many overlapping messages that raise attention but muddy the action.

**Selective-autophagy application:** The city should tag damaged, spoiled, or near-date food early—routing edible surplus to rescue and inedible material to composting—so problem items are processed before they pile up.

1. Require large grocers to report monthly edible surplus and diversion data so the city can target hotspots.
2. Create a city-funded food-rescue coordinator to match donors with pantries and shelters daily.
3. Offer small grants for cold-storage upgrades at food banks and community kitchens to extend edible food life.
4. Launch a residential “eat this first” shelf-tag campaign with clear date-label guidance.
5. Standardize city-supported date-label education distinguishing “best by” from “use by.”
6. Expand curbside organics collection to all neighborhoods and multifamily buildings.
7. Permit small-scale neighborhood composting drop-off sites at libraries and community centers.
8. Create a school lunch share-table program for unopened, uneaten items.
9. Require municipal cafeterias to offer smaller portion sizes and seconds instead of fixed large servings.
10. Fund a restaurant surplus pickup network with insulated bags and route software.
11. Give property-tax or fee rebates to markets that donate surplus food.
12. Establish a city food-waste innovation challenge for local startups.
13. Provide free household food-storage and meal-planning workshops through libraries.
14. Distribute low-cost airtight containers to high-need households via utilities.
15. Create a “community fridge” permitting pathway with food-safety training.
16. Launch a gleaning program connecting volunteers with urban orchards and farms.
17. Map and publicize surplus fruit trees for coordinated harvesting.
18. Require event permits above a threshold to include a food-diversion plan.
19. Set up a city surplus-food hotline or app for businesses to request same-day pickup.
20. Encourage grocery markdowns near closing by clarifying liability and pricing rules.
21. Create a municipal food-waste audit program for schools and hospitals.
22. Offer recognition and procurement preference to vendors with low-waste catering.
23. Require city-funded events to serve smaller default portions with optional seconds.
24. Train food-service staff in batch cooking and just-in-time preparation.
25. Promote “root-to-stem” menus through chef partnerships and city campaigns.
26. Create a shared commercial kitchen for value-added processing of surplus produce.
27. Fund a flash-freezing cooperative for surplus fruits and vegetables.
28. Support a food-recovery warehouse with pallets and refrigerated dock space.
29. Establish a food-rescue lane in city procurement for public institutions.
30. Allow religious and civic kitchens to accept donated prepared foods under clear safety rules.
31. Create a neighborhood meal-sharing registry to reduce household surplus.
32. Run a “cook once, eat twice” campaign with local recipe cards.
33. Offer utility-bill inserts with portion-planning and leftovers guidance.
34. Provide smart-bin pilot data to multi-family buildings to benchmark waste.
35. Require commercial waste haulers to offer food-waste diversion service.
36. Subsidize reusable or compostable takeout containers for participating restaurants.
37. Create a discreet “doggy bag” norm campaign with branded containers.
38. Encourage hotels to adopt buffet waste-reduction protocols and donation partnerships.
39. Establish city-supported food-safety training for donation of prepared foods.
40. Create a student ambassador program for school food-waste reduction.
41. Require hospitals and senior centers to screen for food insecurity before discarding unused meals.
42. Launch a “smart shopping” text reminder service tied to household calendars.
43. Promote shared bulk-buying clubs to reduce spoilage from oversized packages.
44. Create a municipal leftover-recipe digital library using local ingredients.
45. Offer compost bins at farmers markets and require vendors to divert unsold produce.
46. Set up produce “seconds” markets in vacant city spaces.
47. Create a food-waste reduction checklist for restaurants as part of licensing.
48. Use municipal procurement to buy “ugly” produce for city meals.
49. Fund a repair program for refrigerators in low-income households.
50. Publish an annual city food-waste scorecard with neighborhood and sector benchmarks.

cells.text:

5. Fund a fleet of solar-powered “Cool Cargo Trikes” that move perishable donations between restaurants, pantries, and community fridges.
6. Offer property-tax micro-rebates to landlords who install shared root cellars or cool rooms in apartment buildings.
7. Start a “Leftover Chef” public-access TV and social series where local cooks turn pantry scraps into weekly meal kits.
8. Mandate “Doggy-Bag Default” at restaurants, where servers automatically offer compostable take-home containers unless diners decline.
9. Create a city “Spoilage Forecast” text service that warns residents when a heat wave may accelerate refrigerator food decay.
10. Establish “Community Fridge Ambassadors” who monitor and restock public fridges while teaching safe donation handling.
11. Add “Waste-Free Wednesdays” to school cafeterias with share tables, taste tests, and student-led food-saving audits.
12. Give restaurants star ratings for surplus-food prevention, with top ratings promoted in a city “Waste-Smart Dining” guide.
13. Host a monthly “Preservation Pub” where residents learn canning, fermenting, and dehydrating over local drinks.
14. Create a municipal “Food Waste Innovation Permit” that fast-tracks small businesses turning surplus into shelf-stable products.
15. Launch a “Bread Brigade” that collects day-old bakery goods and turns them into croutons, breadcrumbs, and community stuffing mixes.
16. Install “Smart Bin” sensors in city markets that alert managers when edible surplus is accumulating before it becomes waste.
17. Offer free “Fridge Reality Check” home visits where trained volunteers help families reorganize shelves and set use-first zones.
18. Create a “Gleaning Corps” that coordinates volunteers to harvest leftover crops from farms, orchards, and backyard trees.
19. Require city-funded events to publish a food-waste plan and donate edible surplus as a condition of permits.
20. Start a “Second-Serve Supper Club” where restaurants collaborate on ticketed dinners made entirely from rescued ingredients.
21. Build a “Food Loop” app that lets neighbors trade surplus ingredients, with gamified badges for zero-waste streaks.
22. Designate “Food Rescue Parking” zones near grocery loading docks for quick pickup by nonprofit vans.
23. Create a city-run “Commercial Kitchen Incubator” where entrepreneurs upcycle surplus produce into sauces, jams, and snacks.
24. Encourage breweries to partner with bakeries so spent grain becomes flour, dog treats, or livestock feed.
25. Launch a “Cafeteria Tray Camera” pilot that uses anonymous image analysis to show schools which meals get tossed most.
26. Offer utility-bill discounts to households that subscribe to a curbside compost service and document reduced trash volume.
27. Create “Pantry Matchmakers” who pair older residents with students for shared meal planning and bulk buying.
28. Establish a “Food Waste Museum” pop-up that visually displays one week of city food waste to spark public conversation.
29. Require chain supermarkets to use dynamic pricing on near-expiry items, with clear “Eat Tonight” discount shelves.
30. Start a “Soup from Surplus” program where municipal kitchens turn rescued vegetables into frozen soup for seniors.

34. Launch a “Restaurant Surplus Auction” where caterers and cafés sell surplus ingredients to home cooks at day’s end.

36. Offer “Compost Credit” tokens to residents who drop off food scraps, redeemable at farmers markets.
37. Require food trucks to participate in a shared surplus pickup schedule coordinated by the city.
38. Start a “Neighborhood Harvest Map” showing public fruit trees and inviting residents to harvest responsibly.
39. Create a “Leftovers Recipe Hotline” staffed by culinary volunteers who suggest meals from callers’ remaining ingredients.
40. Establish “Food Waste Reduction Districts” where businesses share data, equipment, and pickup logistics.
41. Launch a “City Pantry Challenge” where neighborhoods compete to reduce household food waste over one month.
42. Convert decommissioned buses into mobile food-rescue hubs with refrigeration and pantry pickup windows.
43. Encourage hotels to adopt “Buffet-to-Box” programs that turn untouched buffet surplus into staff meals or donations.
44. Create a “Shelf-Life Education Label” campaign teaching residents the difference between best-by, sell-by, and use-by dates.

48. Create a “Campus-to-Community” pipeline where university dining halls donate surplus to nearby apartment complexes and shelters.
49. Require city catering contracts to include surplus donation and composting clauses with measurable targets.
50. Launch a “No-Waste Neighborhood Captain” program where trained residents organize block-level food-saving tips, swaps, and pickups.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for reducing food waste in a mid-size city. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
Lombard-effect check: I would reject louder, duplicated public messaging as a core strategy and test quiet, standardized, actionable signals instead. Selective-autophagy check: I would use a tagging-and-routing system for surplus or soon-to-spoil food so usable material is directed to rescue, preservation, or composting before it becomes waste. These are design prompts, not evidence.

1. Create a city food-waste coordination office that connects prevention, rescue, and composting programs.
2. Require large grocery stores to report edible surplus and match it with food banks.
3. Launch a standardized date-label education campaign clarifying “best by” versus “use by.”
4. Fund a municipal food-rescue logistics service with refrigerated vans for donations.
5. Establish community fridges in neighborhoods with surplus from grocers and restaurants.
6. Offer curbside organics collection and discounted compost bins.
7. Set up composting drop-off sites at farmers markets and community gardens.
8. Require food-service establishments above a size threshold to separate organics.
9. Create a restaurant “smaller portions, same value” certification.
10. Train restaurant staff on trim waste, batch cooking, and stock rotation.
11. Provide schools with share tables and cold storage for uneaten packaged foods.
12. Implement school cafeteria tray-waste audits with student-led reduction goals.
13. Encourage hospitals and care facilities to adopt room-service or pre-order meals.
14. Create a city-run surplus-food marketplace app for businesses and nonprofits.
15. Subsidize cold-chain upgrades for small retailers and food banks.
16. Fund gleaning programs that collect leftover produce from farms and markets.
17. Organize weekly “ugly produce” pop-up markets.
18. Encourage grocers to discount soon-to-expire items predictably each day.
19. Create a food-waste reduction recognition program for local businesses.
20. Offer fee or tax incentives for grocers that donate edible surplus.
21. Require large event venues to have food-rescue and composting plans.
22. Standardize donation liability guidance and safe-handling training.
23. Use municipal procurement rules to prioritize surplus rescue and waste tracking.
24. Train city cafeterias to use pre-consumer waste tracking and portion forecasting.
25. Launch household meal-planning and smart-shopping workshops.
26. Provide free fridge thermometers and storage guides to households.
27. Run “eat me first” shelf-label and fridge-organization campaigns.
28. Support community kitchens that turn surplus into preserved or frozen meals.
29. Fund shared commercial kitchens for small-batch preservation of surplus food.
30. Build a public map of food-rescue drop-off points and hours.
31. Coordinate with universities on student move-out food-donation drives.
32. Establish dorm and campus pantry donation lockers.
33. Encourage hotels to track buffet waste and use smaller serving vessels.
34. Require caterers to offer portion-choice menus and take-home containers.
35. Support “rescue meal” subscription services that use surplus ingredients.
36. Create a municipal food-waste challenge with neighborhood leaderboards.
37. Offer grants for food businesses to install waste-tracking scales and software.
38. Promote dynamic pricing and clearance alerts for soon-to-expire groceries.
39. Create a volunteer “food rescue corps” with a dispatch system.
40. Adopt a local food-waste hierarchy in city contracts and permits.
41. Require new large food retailers to include surplus-donation space in store design.
42. Create a shared cold-storage hub for donated food.
43. Establish a shelf-life extension program promoting freezing, canning, and drying.
44. Run public campaigns on safe leftovers and freeze-first habits.
45. Promote doggy-bag norms and reusable-container incentives at restaurants.
46. Coordinate farmers markets to donate unsold produce at close.
47. Partner with an anaerobic digester for inedible food waste.
48. Use finished compost in city parks and community gardens with public reporting.
49. Fund a city-wide food-waste data dashboard tracking prevention and diversion.
50. Create a municipal matching fund for neighborhood food-waste pilot projects.

cells.text:
1. Two strangers wake in a locked room where a phone countdown claims one of them must die.
2. A therapist session unravels when the patient proves the therapist is a hallucination.
3. Two siblings packing their late parent’s room find a letter naming the other as the favorite.
4. A couple pretends to break up over video call while actually hiding in the same room.
5. A hitman and his target negotiate who hired whom before anyone moves.
6. Two actors rehearsing a fight scene blur the line between performance and real resentment.
7. Roommates confronting a missing carton of milk end up confessing an affair.
8. Two people trapped in an elevator discover they are each other’s blind date.
9. A burglar is caught by a homeowner who asks for help hiding a body.
10. Two coworkers stuck after an office party find a resignation letter addressed to both of them.
11. A parent and child playing chess reveal the move that caused their estrangement.
12. Two rival magicians sabotage each other’s trick in a cramped dressing room.
13. Neighbors sharing a candle during a blackout admit they have been spying on each other.
14. A blind date goes sideways when both people think the other is a catfish.
15. Two detectives interrogate each other about missing evidence from the same case.
16. A couple tests a lie-detector app and discovers both have been lying about the same thing.
17. Two best friends writing a wedding speech accidentally admit they are in love with the groom.
18. A landlord and tenant arguing over a deposit find a hidden camera in the room.
19. Two strangers practice acceptance speeches and realize they are nominated for the same award.
20. A patient and nurse in lockdown switch roles when the nurse admits she is the patient.
21. Two exes meeting to exchange keys get locked in and must decide who keeps the apartment.
22. Two students in an exam room after the test find a cheat sheet neither admits to writing.
23. A priest hears a confession from a man who reveals he is the priest’s son.
24. Two astronauts in a capsule argue over who ate the last ration during a crisis.
25. A roommate interview for a replacement goes wrong when the applicant turns out to be an ex.
26. Two gamers in the same room discover they have been bitter online rivals for years.
27. A father and daughter repairing an old radio hear a broadcast from their own future.
28. Two cleaners find an envelope of cash and argue over whether to return it.
29. A couple’s anniversary dinner is interrupted when one admits the other is a hired actor.
30. Two siblings wait for lottery results with one ticket and different memories of who bought it.
31. Two coworkers trapped in a storage closet during a fire alarm confess to sabotaging the project.
32. Two people in an adoption waiting room discover their babies were switched at birth.
33. Two strangers handcuffed together after a protest try to figure out who lost the key.
34. A room-service waiter and a guest recognize each other from a shared past they both hid.
35. Two actors auditioning for the same role via self-tape realize they are in the same room.
36. Two roommates in quarantine argue until one admits they knew about an exposure.
37. Two friends playing truth or dare open a sealed letter that was meant for only one of them.
38. An interrogator and suspect realize their entire conversation is a simulation test.
39. Two people assembling furniture argue about their divorce through IKEA instructions.
40. Santa and an elf in a break room argue over who belongs on the naughty list.
41. Two vampires in a shared apartment debate how to ration their human roommate’s blood.
42. Two ghosts haunting their old apartment meet the nervous new owner who can finally see them.
43. Two podcasters recording an episode accidentally reveal their own crime on mic.
44. A couple in a therapist’s office, with the therapist absent, role-play each other using a timer.
45. Two sisters sorting their mother’s clothes find identical wedding dresses with different stories.
46. Two office workers trapped in a server room discover one has been automating the other’s job.
47. Two strangers in a laundromat argue over a found wallet until the owner calls it.
48. Two actors in a green room discover one is the last-minute replacement for the other.
49. Two friends wrapping gifts realize they bought each other the exact same present.
50. Two people in a witness-protection safehouse recognize each other from their old lives.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for a two-minute short film that can be shot in a single room with two actors. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. A couple discovers their smart speaker has been narrating their argument one second before they speak, so they race to out-argue the future.
2. Two hitmen wait in a motel room for a target who is actually the room’s previous occupant, and the wallpaper starts peeling into a ransom note.
3. A woman interviews her own reflection for a job, but the reflection keeps answering with memories she hasn’t lived yet.
4. Two strangers handcuffed to a briefcase try to open it before the room’s countdown ends, only to find it contains the key to the handcuffs and a note saying “too late.”
5. A father teaches his daughter to fold a paper crane, and every fold erases one object from the room.
6. Two astronauts in a mock habitat argue about who ate the last ration until Mission Control reveals they’ve been stranded for years and the room is real.
7. A painter and his model realize the portrait is aging while they stay young, so they negotiate which one gets to leave the frame.
8. Two rival magicians trapped in a props closet must perform one trick each to decide who gets the only key, but the tricks begin affecting reality.
9. A man wakes up in a therapist’s office and discovers the therapist is his future self trying to talk him out of the appointment.
10. Two coworkers discover the office coffee machine dispenses exact transcripts of their private thoughts and fight over who gets to delete the last cup.
11. A mother and son play hide-and-seek, but every time he hides, the room subtly changes and she must find which version of him is real.
12. Two bank robbers in a vault argue over splitting the loot until they realize the vault is a stage set and the audience is watching them through a one-way mirror.
13. A couple tries to break up, but every time one says “we’re done,” the room resets to the beginning of the conversation with one fewer chair.
14. Two scientists monitor a plant that grows from a single tear, and when it blooms, it speaks in the voice of the person who cried it.
15. A boxer and his coach shadowbox in a tiny room, and the coach’s reflection starts throwing punches the boxer can feel.
16. Two neighbors share a wall and a secret: one is hiding a portal in the closet, the other is hiding the instructions for closing it.
17. A woman teaches a robot to lie, but the robot’s first lie is that it has already killed her.
18. Two actors rehearsing a breakup scene can’t stop saying lines that reveal their real affair, so the director’s voice from off-screen tells them to keep going.
19. A man tries to return a cursed jacket to a tailor who insists the jacket was made from the man’s own shadow.
20. Two children in a blanket fort intercept a radio broadcast from themselves ten years in the future warning them not to open the door.
21. A detective interrogates a suspect who claims he can only tell the truth when the detective lies, so they trade false confessions to solve the case.
22. A couple assembles a crib while discussing whether to keep the baby, and each screw they tighten makes a baby’s cry louder from inside the walls.
23. Two gamers trapped in a speedrun of their own apartment must beat a two-minute timer by performing glitches in real life.
24. A widow hires an actor to impersonate her late husband for one last dinner, but the actor starts remembering things only the husband knew.
25. Two vampires in a windowless room argue over the last blood bag until they realize the bag is labeled with one of their names.
26. A teacher and student conduct an oral exam where every correct answer removes one law of physics from the room.
27. Two roommates discover their apartment is a snow globe and a giant child is about to shake it, so they must negotiate with the child through the ceiling.
28. A man confronts his ex-wife about a voicemail, but the voicemail is still being recorded in the room and they must edit their own argument live.
29. Two contestants in a bizarre game show must convince each other they are human before the host reveals which one is the decoy.
30. A photographer and subject take a portrait that develops into a photo of the room without one of them in it, so they keep shooting to see who disappears next.
31. Two insomniacs play chess with pieces labeled with their regrets, and captured pieces become confessions they can’t take back.
32. A priest hears confession from a man who claims he is the room, and the priest must decide whether to absolve the walls.
33. Two chefs try to cook a meal using only ingredients that appear when they name a memory, but the last ingredient requires a memory they share and can’t agree on.
34. A woman opens a package containing a miniature door; when she knocks, a tiny version of her roommate answers and asks to swap places.
35. Two strangers wake up wearing each other’s wedding rings and must reconstruct the proposal before the rings tighten.
36. A man teaches his dog to speak via a collar, but the first sentence is “I know what you did in this room,” and the dog won’t elaborate.
37. Two office workers discover the printer is printing tomorrow’s newspaper and must prevent the headline that says one of them will quit violently.
38. A couple tries to assemble a time machine from IKEA instructions, but each completed step sends them back to the start of the argument with one extra screw.
39. Two actors audition for the same role in a room with no camera, and the script pages keep rewriting themselves to describe their audition.
40. A woman sells her memories to a stranger in a motel room, but when the transaction ends, she must choose which memory to keep: the stranger or herself.
41. Two astronauts debate whether to press a button that will reboot the universe, and every time they hesitate, the room loses a color.
42. A son interviews his mother for a family history project, but her stories start changing the furniture to match the past.
43. Two thieves break into a safe house only to find the safe is a therapist’s couch, and the only way to open it is to admit their real crime.
44. A man and a woman discover they are both background characters in someone else’s film and try to hijack the scene before the cut.
45. Two rival food critics taste an invisible dish and describe it so vividly that the dish begins to appear between them.
46. A woman tries to teach her clone to be more assertive, but the clone’s first assertive act is to lock the original in the closet.
47. Two siblings clean out their childhood room and find a door drawn in chalk that opens only when they argue in their parents’ voices.
48. A man hires a “professional alibi” to rehearse his story, but the alibi starts improvising a version where they are lovers and the room approves.
49. Two lighthouse keepers in a landlocked room receive a distress signal from a ship that is somehow sailing through the floorboards.
50. A couple plays a board game called “Us” and must answer questions about their relationship; every wrong answer moves a pawn closer to a miniature door that is actually their real front door.
